pack.title: Unit 7.0 Explaining Application Services
pack.notes: WIP: written without class materials; needs a pass once they are made.

flashcards.definition: The relational database platform that clients connect to over TCP port 1433.
An appliance dedicated to the file server role, reached by IP address, that copies and backs up data at file level with protocols such as SMB; it shares bandwidth with other network traffic.
A hardware appliance or software instance that spreads client requests across a pool of servers doing the same job, so the service can scale and stay fault tolerant.
The family of protocols, such as HSRP and VRRP, that let several routers share one virtual IP address as a subnet's default gateway, so hosts keep a gateway if one router fails.
The single address that clients use to reach a cluster or a group of routers; the active device owns it, and another device takes it over if that one fails.
The most data loss a system can sustain, measured as the time between the last good backup and the disaster.
The longest an individual IT system may stay offline after a disaster, covering both finding the problem and restoring from backup or switching in another system.
The average time it takes to correct a fault and restore a system to full operation.
The expected lifetime of a product that can be repaired, such as a server.
An alternate site that takes longest to set up: it may be an empty building with a lease agreement to install the needed equipment when necessary.
An alternate site with operational equipment in place, but the latest dataset must be loaded before services can fail over to it.
An alternate site that can take over almost immediately, with operational equipment kept updated with a live dataset.
A cluster in which every node handles connections at once, using the hardware's full capacity, but performance drops when a node fails and the rest take on its workload.
A cluster in which a standby node sits unused until the working node fails, so performance holds during failover, but the unused capacity can raise costs.
Teams discussing and working through a hypothetical disaster scenario to assess their response plans and decision-making and find gaps in knowledge, communication, and coordination.
Performing simulated failovers to prove that services can be restored from backup configurations and data, and to measure recovery time.
Synchronizes clocks to within nanoseconds, where NTP manages milliseconds, for the most timing-critical networks.
Protects NTP with TLS against unauthorized time sources and manipulated time data.
The most widely used mail retrieval protocol, letting clients manage a mailbox kept on the server, with several clients on one mailbox at once; SMTP only delivers the mail.
Uses a server's digital certificate to authenticate it and then encrypts the TCP connection, turning HTTP into HTTPS; it was developed from the older SSL, which is now obsolete.
The older protocol that TLS was developed from; it is now completely obsolete.
Protects an FTP session with an SSL/TLS tunnel that is set up before any FTP commands are sent; SFTP uses SSH instead.
An NTP server's distance from an accurate clock source: servers linked directly to the clock are at level 1, and each network step away adds one level.
An automated switchboard that connects calls between endpoints over the local IP network and routes calls to and from outside networks through a service provider.
The end-user device that a person uses to place and receive VoIP calls.
Cisco's proprietary protocol in which a group of routers shares one virtual IP as the default gateway: the active router answers, and the router with the next highest priority waits to take over.
The open standard protocol in which a master router answers as the default gateway on a shared virtual IP, every other router is a backup, and no router needs its own unique IP address.
Plans and tasks for specific large-scale outages that threaten a whole site, such as switching services to failover systems or sites and restoring systems and data from backups.
Keeping the same, or nearly the same, level of service when individual components fail, usually through redundancy, such as RAID, UPSs, or clusters, that removes single points of failure.
Switching automatically to a redundant component, path, or node when the one in use fails, so the system keeps operating normally.
Linking redundant nodes that share data with one another so clients see one server on a shared virtual IP; if a node stops working, its connections fail over to another.
The most cost-effective recovery option for many companies: moving processing and data storage to a provider whose datacenters in other regions keep services running through a local disaster.
The expected lifetime of a component that cannot be repaired, such as a hard drive.
